title: Flowers on the Wrench
hookLine: night nine: auto-rickshaws wear garlands, a mechanic puts a flower on his wrench, and the last name in the list is the giver of accomplishment
carry: work offered to God becomes worship
tomorrow: can anyone find the end of a pillar of fire?

cards: An auto-rickshaw parked outside a temple, with a garland of marigolds across its windshield and a smear of turmeric on the bumper.

A mechanic's shop where the wrenches have been wiped clean, laid in a row and given a flower each. A tailor's sewing machine with a red dot on it. A laptop, closed, with a sprig of something green on the lid.
In parts of South India, the ninth day of Navaratri is Ayudha Puja, the worship of tools. Where it's kept, the tools aren't worked with today. They're cleaned, thanked and honored.

teach.b: The ninth name in the Kavacha's list, the last one, is Siddhidatri, the giver of siddhi: accomplishment, the power to bring a thing to completion. On this night she's shown seated on a lotus, calm.
Now put her beside the mechanic. Where does accomplishment come from? Hindus have an old answer, near the end of the Bhagavad Gita.

teach.h: THE GITA: SIDDHI THROUGH YOUR OWN WORK.
teach.b: Krishna says a person reaches siddhi, the same word, by worshiping the one from whom all beings come, through their own work. Not by leaving the shop for the temple. By the work itself, offered.
That's the teaching Ayudha Puja acts out once a year.

teach.h: THE TOOLS REST ON THE ALTAR.
teach.b: The wrench, the sewing machine, the pen, the stove, the laptop are how a life serves, so for a day they're cleaned, rested and honored like anything else on an altar. Look back over the nine nights.

The goddess came as the mountain's daughter, a smile that made a world, a mother with her child, a warrior named for a sage, night itself, the bright one washed clean, and now the giver of accomplishment.

teach.h: THE AUTUMN WORSHIP AND THE BOOK.
teach.b: Near the end of the Devi Mahatmya, the goddess herself speaks of the great worship offered to her in autumn, and says that whoever hears her story then, with devotion, will be freed from troubles by her grace.
Tomorrow the year turns to Shiva, and to the Shiva Purana.

how: In parts of South India, Ayudha Puja on the ninth day of Navaratri honors tools, vehicles, machines and instruments, which are cleaned, decorated and rested; where the nine forms are kept, the ninth night honors Siddhidatri, and the next day is Vijayadashami.

games.q: what does “navaratri as a nine-night curriculum” mean?
o: nine ordered nights that end by honoring the tools of work
nine nights that end with every tool put away for good
nine nights that end with a wish for new tools and wealth

games.q: the nine nights — tap the pairs.
p: reached through your own work, the Gita says

s: on Ayudha Puja, people work extra hard with their tools
the tools rest. they're cleaned, decorated and honored, not used.
in the Devi Mahatmya, the goddess speaks of an autumn worship
she says whoever hears her story then, with devotion, will be freed from troubles.
in the Gita, siddhi comes only by leaving your work for the temple
Krishna says a person reaches it by worshiping God through their own work.

games.q: it's Ayudha Puja in a mechanic's shop. a customer pulls in with a flat tire. what's the custom with the wrenches today?
o: use them as usual; it's a normal day.
they rest, cleaned and garlanded, honored for the day.
games.why: on Ayudha Puja the tools rest and are honored. the work they do all year is offered to God, so today they get the flowers.

practice: One by one, bring to mind the things your hands use to get through a day, keys, a phone, a pan, a pen, a keyboard, a steering wheel, a broom, and give each a moment of thanks, the way the mechanic gives each wrench a flower.
Then let the hands themselves come to mind, resting in your lap; they're tools too. If you pray, you can offer tomorrow's work to the goddess, or to God, in your own words.
If you don't, simply decide to do one piece of it well, as a gift.

wordCard.voice: Navaratri, night nine: Siddhidatri, the giver of accomplishment, and the day the tools rest and are honored.

orig.note: Sanskrit: Siddhidatri, the ninth of the nine forms named in the Devi Kavacha.

carryVoice: Your line: work offered to God becomes worship. A flower on every wrench. The goddess's part, complete.
